title: US Treasury Intervenes in Long-Bond Market as Bessent Doubles Buyback Programme
summary: The US Treasury announced it would at least double the size of its long-dated bond buyback operations — lifting the maximum per-operation ceiling from $2 billion to at least $4 billion — as the 30-year yield approached a 20-year high. The significance lies not in the yield move itself but in what the intervention reveals: when the market chronically demands a premium the fiscal trajectory cannot justify, the sovereign issuer becomes the buyer of last resort for its own debt, a line that had not been crossed at this scale since the programme was restarted in 2024.
context:
- The Treasury buyback programme was relaunched in May 2024 for the first time since 2002, initially framed as a routine liquidity-support mechanism for off-the-run bonds; deploying it at scale to cap long-end yields crosses into territory that blurs the line between technical market management and de facto yield-curve control, historically the province of the Federal Reserve.

- A confluence of structural forces has pushed the long end higher in a way that short-term rate policy cannot address: a persistently wide fiscal deficit, inflation above the Fed's 2% target for five consecutive years, a weakening dollar, and a surge of corporate bond issuance by technology companies financing AI infrastructure that competes directly with Treasuries for long-duration buyers.

- The initial doubling failed almost immediately: bond yields erased the relief rally within 24 hours, forcing Bessent to signal on CNBC the following day that buybacks could be expanded well beyond $4 billion — an admission that the structural supply-demand imbalance in long bonds is deeper than a single operational adjustment can resolve.

- The episode echoes earlier episodes of fiscal-monetary tension: in 1951 the Fed-Treasury Accord ended a wartime yield-cap arrangement; today's buyback escalation raises the question of whether, without formal coordination, the Treasury is informally taking on the long-end management role the Fed has stepped away from since it ended quantitative easing.

- For investors, the key structural implication is that US long-dated debt is increasingly priced by a combination of fiscal supply, central bank passivity, and discretionary Treasury intervention — a regime shift that makes duration risk harder to model and traditionally 'safe' long bonds behave more like managed instruments than free-market instruments.

title: China's July Data Miss Points to a Structural Demand Problem, Not a Cyclical Dip
summary: China's July activity data, released on 17 August, missed forecasts across every major indicator: industrial output slowed to 4.5% year-on-year from 5.3% in June, retail sales rose just 0.6% against a forecast of 1.5%, and fixed-asset investment contracted 6.7% in the first seven months of 2026. The breadth of the miss matters more than any single number — it signals that China's growth model is increasingly constrained by a structural shortfall in domestic demand rather than a temporary cyclical weakness that policy stimulus can smooth over.
context:
- China's property sector has been contracting for four years and remains the economy's deepest structural wound: real estate historically accounted for roughly a quarter of economic activity and is the primary store of household wealth, so a prolonged downturn suppresses both consumer confidence and the collateral value that underpins local-government and corporate borrowing.

- Exports have provided a surface-level offset — growing 23.1% in July — but the headline strength reflects tariff front-loading ahead of anticipated further US and EU measures rather than genuine end-demand growth; this pattern mechanically reverses once those measures are implemented, making export growth a borrowed rather than a durable source of GDP momentum.

- The full-year trade surplus is on course to exceed $1 trillion for a second consecutive year, a record that has intensified geopolitical pressure from both Washington, which announced fresh targeted tariffs on Chinese goods during the week, and Brussels, which is now formally weighing additional barriers — meaning the export channel that has been propping up growth faces structural compression from multiple directions.

- Fixed-asset investment contracting 6.7% in the year to July signals a loss of private-sector confidence even as central government stimulus continues to be rolled out; businesses and local governments are pulling back in parallel with Beijing's push, a divergence that conventional monetary easing cannot close because it does not address the underlying confidence and balance-sheet problem.

- The structural mismatch — strong production capacity and exports alongside anaemic domestic consumption — cannot be resolved quickly because it requires a redistribution of income toward households, reform of the social safety net to reduce precautionary saving, and a resolution of property-sector debt overhangs, all of which are politically and economically complex for Beijing to execute simultaneously.

title: Markets Brace for Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole Debut as FOMC Turns Hawkish
summary: The Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, scheduled for 27–29 August, has become the dominant market event of the week as investors try to read how Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh — appointed by President Trump and making his first major address as chair — will frame the inflation and rate-hike debate. July's FOMC meeting passed by a hawkish 9–3 vote, the most divided the committee has been since 2022, and markets entered the week pricing roughly one-in-three odds of a September rate hike. The background question is whether a new Fed leadership with a different institutional philosophy will treat stubborn inflation as reason enough to resume tightening even as economic growth shows signs of strain.
context:
- Kevin Warsh served as a Fed Governor during the 2008 financial crisis and has long been a public sceptic of the central bank's quantitative-easing era, arguing that prolonged asset-purchase programmes distorted market pricing and delayed necessary economic adjustments; his appointment by President Trump signalled an administration preference for a chair more willing to prioritise inflation-fighting over growth protection.

- The federal funds rate has been held at 3.50–3.75% since December 2025, pausing a cutting cycle that began in late 2024 after inflation proved more durable than expected; July CPI at 3.4% year-on-year — more than a percentage point above the Fed's 2% target — means the cutting rationale has weakened without a clear tightening mandate emerging either, trapping the committee in an uncomfortable hold.

- The tariff-driven component of US inflation complicates the Fed's task structurally: if price pressure is supply-side and import-cost driven rather than demand-driven, raising rates reduces inflation only at the cost of suppressing economic activity more severely, giving the central bank a narrower policy corridor than a demand-driven inflationary episode would present.

- Jackson Hole has historically been the forum where Fed chairs have signalled their most consequential pivot moments — Bernanke's effective preview of QE2 in 2010, Powell's blunt 2022 speech that told markets rate hikes would be sustained whatever the growth cost — which is why markets treat Warsh's twenty minutes at the podium as a potential policy tiebreaker for the September meeting.

- A September rate hike, if it materialises, would be the first tightening move since July 2023 and would arrive against a backdrop of already-elevated long-term yields, meaning the Fed would be adding to borrowing-cost pressure at both the short and long end simultaneously — a combination that tends to compress credit conditions faster than a conventional rate-hike cycle.
